California’s ‘orphaned’ ballot measures
By WILL MCCARTHY (https://www.politico.com/staff/will-mccarthy), JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white) and NICOLE NORMAN (https://www.politico.com/staff/nicole-norman)
10/05/2026 03:09 PM EDT
State Sen. Josh Newman talks during a Senate session in Sacramento, California, on June 11, 2018. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
LEFT BEHIND: Over the last two and a half years, California lawmakers spent countless hours drafting, debating and voting on a group of government reform ballot measures to put before voters. The same energy has not been put toward campaigns to pass them.
Proposition 5, which would change how successors are chosen in recalls, was set for the ballot way back in August 2024. Proposition 4, which would allow for the public financing of campaigns, landed in October 2025. Proposition 2, which would double the amount the state can deposit into its reserves, was rushed to the November ballot earlier this spring.
All aim to reform a somewhat wonky aspect of how government operates, and none of them are easily explainable to voters in a single sentence. And yet each of them have a limited, or non-existent public presence and campaign.
“You get these orphaned initiatives,” said Thad Kousser , a professor of political science at the University of San Diego. “So voters are left with very few bits of information on what’s going to be the most crowded ballot in a decade.”
The recall measure’s travails underscore how quickly a political window can close. In the aftermath of the failed attempt to recall Gov. Gavin Newsom , triumphant Democrats said they were determined to change a system that would allow a challenger — like MAGA tribune Larry Elder (https://www.politico.com/news/2021/08/17/ca-recall-election-larry-elder-505735) — to become governor with fewer votes than the number cast against a recall. Secretary of State Shirley Weber vowed action (https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/09/15/california-elections-chief-wants-recall-overhaul-possibly-as-soon-as-2022-1391082), and election committees revved up (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2021/09/16/with-newsom-secure-democrats-look-to-restrain-recall-494353).
But the momentum soon ebbed. Policymakers couldn’t agree on the changes. Polls showed voters were tepid on changing a process that many see as an important check on elected officials. By the time former State Sen. Josh Newman finally got his measure through, the Newsom recall — and the sense of urgency it engendered — were distant memories.
A spokesperson for the Prop 5 campaign did not reply to requests for comment, although Newman said in a recent interview that he was “not optimistic” about the recall reform measure’s chances.
Historically, the vast majority of measures placed on the ballot by the legislature have won — a full 69% between 1910 and 2025. In the past, that outcome has been largely a function of how many votes it takes for lawmakers to put measures before voters, a two-thirds majority of both houses traditionally meaning that the issue was highly popular.
But polling for the three government reform measures is scattershot. A September Public Policy Institute of California poll had Prop 4 and Prop 5 with only 42% and 35% support, respectively, while Prop 2 had the support of 60% of voters (a later Berkeley IGS poll put Prop 4’s support at 35% for, 35% against, and 30% undecided).
Prop 5 does not appear to have any financial backing or a campaign committee organized to pass the measure. The committee for Prop 4 has a single, $235,000 contribution from Movement Voter PAC, a progressive organizing group. Prop 2’s committee received a $150,000 contribution from Google last week.
Assemblymember Alex Lee , one of the coauthors of the legislation that placed Prop 4 on the ballot, said the measure was in a “good place” and that undecided voters are “ready to be persuaded.” The Prop 4 campaign has begun holding public events and is planning a bus tour at some point this fall.
“I knew the other marquee efforts would absorb the media attention,” Lee said. “Really it’s just about the voter education campaign.”
Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel , author of Prop 2, said you likely won’t see large ad spends or public appearances to drum up support for expanding the state’s budget reserves. Given the solid polling and what he called the “common sense wisdom” of the measure, he’s confident in its passage.
Meant to shield the state’s budget from the volatility of the stock market, the measure has the support of a wide range of groups, from the California Chamber of Commerce to SEIU. Even so, Gabriel said he expected a “lean campaign” that will “rely a lot on member-to-member communication.”
Each of the government reform measures share at least one key advantage: None face organized opposition.
“Its not like we have to raise X millions of dollars,” Lee said.
Welcome to Ballot Measure Weekly , a special Monday edition of Playbook PM focused on California’s lively realm of ballot measure campaigns. Questions? Concerns? Tips? Drop ballot measures reporter Will McCarthy a line at [email protected] (https://www.politico.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#65120806060417110d1c25150a090c110c060a4b060a08) .
TOP OF THE TICKET
A highly subjective ranking of the ballot measures — past and future, certain and possible — getting our attention this week.
1. Prop 37: The campaign for a measure to provide loans to help middle-income families purchase homes contributed $300,000 to the California Democratic Party last week, apparently viewing the measure in good financial standing.
2. Prop 38: The No on Prop 38 campaign is operating with a single six-figure check as it tries to run a campaign against billionaire Gary Michelson ’s immunology bond ballot measure. The $3,000 contribution comes from Robert Kaplan , the director of research at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center. Michelson has contributed over $10 million to the initiative, which has come under criticism in recent weeks (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).
3. Prop 45: A group of Republican county organizations came out against Prop 45 last week, even as the Yes campaign faced scrutiny for donations (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317427465.html) to Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio ’s Reform California organization (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730). The Yes campaign, meanwhile, released a report (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/) showing what it says would be the “significant economic benefits” of Prop 45, including adding 20,000 homes a year.
4. Fund scientific research (2028): Newsom climbed the Golden Gate Bridge (https://x.com/CAgovernor/status/2105470383281598682) with State Sen. Scott Wiener and a camera crew to sign a $7.5 billion research bond that aims to combat federal funding cuts. The measure will be on the ballot in 2028. “I’m proud to sign a bond to invest in the future of the state of California,” Newsom said in a video from the bridge.
5. Prop 40: Heavily outspent and facing enormous establishment resistance, the wealth tax campaign is hoping America’s most prominent progressive can carry it to victory. Sen. Bernie Sanders is rallying for Prop 40 in Los Angeles today after swinging through San Francisco on Saturday, where he described the campaign as a Democrat-defining battle over “the most important ballot initiative in the country.” (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/03/bernie-sanders-billionaire-tax-san-francisco-rally-01105995)
6. Prop 39: DeMaio is continuing on his “Barbecue, Beer, & Ballots” tour through California, attending his tenth barbecue of the last week in Ramona (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/events/barbeque-beer-ballots-ramona-10-05-2026) today as the campaign looks to help pass Prop 39. As Will wrote for POLITICO Magazine last week (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730?utm_source=firefox-newtab-en-us), DeMaio’s grassroots army has become a major factor in his rise in state politics.
7. Measure ER (Los Angeles County): A one-half cent sales tax narrowly approved by Los Angeles County voters in June took effect on Oct. 1. But it could be a while before the $1 billion it is expected to generate each year for health care can actually be spent. A lawsuit, brought by the Libertarian Party of LA County, will have to play out in LA County Superior Court before the proceeds can be used.
FIRST IN PLAYBOOK — Californians for Voting Rights, one of the committees organized to defeat Prop 39, is launching a pair of advertisements in the Bay Area hammering on the “consequences voters will face” should the measure pass. In the first spot, the No campaign characterizes Prop 39 as a “MAGA power grab” led by President Donald Trump (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cjk5YyP7FYM). The second warns people (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EbT1lgt8ic4) of longer lines in order to vote. The seven-figure buy is the committee’s first time on air.
IN OTHER NEWS
HE’S BACK: Former Gov. Jerry Brown will tonight join journalist Miriam Pawel , the author of nonfiction works about the Brown family (https://miriampawel.com/the-browns-of-california/) and Cesar Chavez (https://www.nytimes.com/2014/04/27/books/review/the-crusades-of-cesar-chavez-by-miriam-pawel.html), for a conversation launching her latest book: “California Dreams: The Making and Remaking of the University of California.” The discussion will “explore the history of the University of California, its relationship with California’s political and social life, and the continuing importance of public higher education,” and the event will run from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. at the California State Library. The retired Brown’s appearance is his latest since he visited the state Capitol during end-of-session proceedings and penned a call for global nuclear (https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2026/10/08/i-taste-ashes-in-the-wind-nuclear-weapons-jerry-brown/) disarmament. Register here (https://libraryca.libcal.com/event/17654368) .
THE BOOGEYMAN: Democrats’ top Senate super PAC is flooding the airwaves with ads hitting Republicans on Jeffrey Epstein, the late financier and convicted sex offender. They have data to back it up, POLITICO’s Andrew Howard reports (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/05/democrats-smp-attack-ads-epstein-01106408).
Internal polling of over 4,500 voters from Senate Majority PAC, conducted by the Democratic firm Blue Rose Research late last week and shared with POLITICO, found that a 44% plurality of voters — including the same percentage of swing voters — think the Epstein issue is “serious” and that Republicans should be held responsible.
And while nothing trumps affordability as the issue du jour on the campaign trail this fall, state-level research from SMP found that the Epstein ads can shift races three to six points in Democrats’ direction.

Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Summary
Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher. Supporters : CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel Opponents : None submitted

What your vote means
Yes
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.

Arguments
Pro
Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
Con
Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.

It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies.
Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).

Of the 164 statewide ballot measures that voters have or will decide this year, there were six that state Democratic and Republican parties agreed on and 70 that they disagreed on.
Fifty-two measures received support or opposition from only one party.
Thirty-six measures did not receive support or opposition from either party.
Republicans supported 50 that Democrats opposed, and Democrats supported 20 that Republicans opposed.

PROP
2
INCREASES STATE’S RAINY DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher. Supporters : CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel Opponents : None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
CON
Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.

## Analysis of Measure
### Background
#### Reserves
***State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.”*** The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state’s main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year.
Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program.
...
### Proposal
***Save More in the Rainy Day Fund.*** Proposition 2 requires the state to make deposits into the rainy day fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
In addition, the state would make even larger deposits in years when revenues from taxes on investment gains are very high, like when the stock market is booming.
...
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change.
As a result, state budget reserves would be higher.
The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.

### Background
#### Reserves
***Reserves Allow the State to Maintain Spending When Revenues Decline.*** The state puts money into reserves when the economy is doing well.
This means that money is saved instead of being spent on public programs during these periods of time.
When the economy gets worse and revenues decline, the state uses reserves to help maintain spending on public programs.
Reserves help the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases, and borrowing to balance the budget.
Currently, the state has about $20 billion in reserves that can be used for any public program.
***State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.”*** The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state’s main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year.
Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program.
In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal.
During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.

PROP
2
INCREASES STATE’S RAINY DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
THE STATE BUDGET
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
How Does the State Raise Revenue? The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for most spending from the General Fund. Other major taxes include the corporation tax and the sales tax. Much of the income tax is paid by high-income taxpayers, whose incomes often include gains from stocks and other investments.
State Revenues Are Unpredictable. State revenues go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because revenues depend on how the economy and stock market are doing. When things are going well, revenues can grow quickly. When things are going badly, like during a recession or a stock market crash, revenues can decline by tens of billions of dollars. During a bad recession or market crash, total revenue declines over a few years can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues.
The State Must Meet Certain Budgeting Requirements Each Year. The State Constitution requires the Legislature to pass a balanced budget each year. This means the state cannot adopt a budget that spends more money than is available. In addition, the State Constitution limits how much tax revenue the state can spend. This limit is called the “state appropriations limit.” Certain kinds of spending—like infrastructure—do not count toward the limit. All other spending, including money put into reserves, does count toward the limit.
RESERVES
Reserves Allow the State to Maintain Spending When Revenues Decline. The state puts money into reserves when the economy is doing well. This means that money is saved instead of being spent on public programs during these periods of time. When the economy gets worse and revenues decline, the state uses reserves to help maintain spending on public programs. Reserves help the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases, and borrowing to balance the budget. Currently, the state has about $20 billion in reserves that can be used for any public program.
State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.” The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state's main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year. Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program. In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal. During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level. Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits. The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).
DEBT
The State Has Different Kinds of Debts. The state has more than $250 billion in debts. These include debt for infrastructure and pension and retiree health benefits earned by state employees. The state also sometimes borrows money from other state funds to help pay General Fund costs. State debts are repaid over time, usually according to a schedule or plan. Each year, the state makes payments toward its debts.
State Constitution Requires the State to Make Extra Debt Payments Toward Pension and Health Benefits. The State Constitution requires the state to make extra debt payments above those normally made each year. The amount of these extra debt payments is the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. The state may only use these extra debt payments to pay down long-term pension and retiree health care debts. Making extra payments toward these debts saves the state money in the long run.
Extra Debt Payments Optional After 2030. The requirement for extra debt payments ends in 2030. After that, the Legislature and the Governor could decide to deposit the money for extra debt payments into the rainy day fund instead. Or, the Legislature and the Governor could make smaller extra debt payments and put the rest of the money into the rainy day fund.
PROPOSAL
Save More in the Rainy Day Fund. Proposition 2 requires the state to make deposits into the rainy day fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of 10 percent of General Fund taxes). In addition, the state would make even larger deposits in years when revenues from taxes on investment gains are very high, like when the stock market is booming.
Extend and Expand Extra Debt Payments. Proposition 2 also requires the state to make extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of through 2030). These debt payments would be the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. In addition, the amount set aside for extra debt payments could be used for an expanded set of purposes. Specifically, these payments could be used to make required payments to schools and community colleges, repay borrowing from other state funds, and repay certain loans from the federal government.
Change How Rainy Day Fund Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. Deposits into the rainy day fund would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out.
Change How Other Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. The state has an account to set aside funds when revenues are surging. By setting these funds aside, the state can avoid overspending when revenue estimates are particularly uncertain. Under Proposition 2, deposits into this account also would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out. This exclusion could not be larger than 10 percent of General Fund taxes in each year.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Budget Reserves Would Be Higher. By continuing to require deposits into the rainy day fund until the balance reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes, the state would save more over time. In addition, by depositing more money when revenues are surging, the state likely would save more in the rainy day fund in certain years. More reserves would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline.
Possibly More Debt Payments. By requiring the state to make extra debt payments through 2040, the state might make more debt payments than it would without Proposition 2.

ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 2
VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 2 TO PROTECT SCHOOLS, HEALTHCARE, PUBLIC SAFETY AND CALIFORNIA'S FINANCIAL FUTURE.
California's Rainy Day Fund, established by voters in 2014, was built for exactly this moment: an economy that swung our state budget from a $100 billion surplus to a $50 billion deficit in just a few years.
Proposition 2 strengthens that fund, so schools, healthcare, and public safety don't pay the price for Sacramento's boom-and-bust budgeting. Voting YES on Proposition 2 will:
DOUBLE THE STATE'S RESERVE REQUIREMENT-from 10 to 20 percent of General Fund revenues-so California has a real cushion, not a token one, when the next downturn hits.
STOP SACRAMENTO POLITICIANS FROM OVERSPENDING-When tax revenues spike, this measure forces politicians to budget smarter by requiring the state to bank more of that windfall instead of committing it to new ongoing spending California can't sustain.
GUARANTEE EDUCATION FUNDING IS PROTECTED IN THE STATE CONSTITUTION, even as reserves grow.
INCREASE FINANCIAL SECURITY-As Washington moves to cut billions in health care and food assistance funding, this measure will ensure California is better prepared to absorb those losses without slashing the programs Californians depend on.
This is not a partisan idea. Republicans and Democrats in the state Legislature and Governor Gavin Newsom support Proposition 2.

Saving for a rainy day is what California families do. It's what California's state government should do too. Vote YES on Proposition 2-and make sure the next time the economy turns, California is ready.

Senate Elections and Constitutional Amendments Committee
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 2
Voting NO on Prop. 2 means more money in your pocket- and less wasteful spending!
PROP. 2 CREATES A SLUSH FUND FOR SACRAMENTO POLITICIANS
In 1978 California voters overwhelmingly voted to amend the state constitution to impose a spending limit on state politicians-and the politicians have hated that spending limit ever since. Prop. 2 allows the politicians to gut the voter-imposed spending limit. What the politicians dishonestly call a “rainy day fund” is actually a SLUSH FUND! Politicians can raid this new slush fund to feed their runaway spending habits.
PROP. 2 CANCELS YOUR TAX REBATE
California already has the highest taxes in the nation, but the state constitution requires that a tax rebate be provided to you when revenues exceed the spending limit. Prop. 2 creates loopholes and accounting gimmicks so politicians can eliminate any chance of you getting your tax rebate.
PROP. 2 ALLOWS FOR MORE WASTEFUL SPENDING
California’s state budget has grown by 76% since 2018-and the size of state government has mushroomed by 40% even after adjusting for inflation! Do you feel like you are getting 40% more services and benefits today than you did in 2018? Of course not! In fact, many core services to citizens have been gutted. We’re spending more, but getting less.
That’s because state politicians have diverted your tax dollars to boondoggle projects and no-bid contracts that reward their campaign contributors. Of the little money spent on important programs, too much of it is being lost because of fraud and wasteful spending. By eliminating the spending limit on politicians we will see even more wasteful spending.
PROP. 2 MAKES OUR BUDGET MORE VOLATILE
When times are good, the state is supposed to set money aside so families and businesses are not hit with tax increases, cuts to essential services, or budget chaos during the next economic downturn. Sacramento doesn’t need a new tool to save money. It needs the discipline to follow the rules already in place and stop spending money it doesn’t have. Prop. 2 makes our budget more volatile- putting us at greater risk of a financial crisis.
PROP. 2 IS OPPOSED BY TRUSTED BUDGET WATCHDOGS
Take a look at who is supporting Prop. 2: politicians who have repeatedly mismanaged our budget and special interests that get government contracts! Within 24 hours of putting it on the ballot, the politicians backing Prop. 2 voted to suspend more than $5 billion in required deposits into the state’s budget reserve. In contrast, opponents of Prop. 2 are government accountability and transparency watchdogs-including the Reform California and the Transparency Foundation. Californians do not need another budget gimmick dressed up as reform. We need honest budgeting, reform of wasteful spending, and a real spending limit to hold politicians accountable.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 2.
David Tangipa , Vice Chair
Assembly Budget Committee
Steven Choi , Vice Chair
Senate Elections and Constitutional Amendment Committee
Carl DeMaio , Chairman
Reform California
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 2
PROPOSITION 2 PROTECTS CALIFORNIANS FROM BOOM-AND-BUST BUDGETS
Opponents say the state needs “discipline,” not a new tool. But relying on their definition of “discipline” alone gave California a $100 billion surplus followed by a $50 billion deficit-exactly the boom-and-bust cycle Proposition 2 is designed to prevent. That instability, not this measure, is what leads to layoffs, healthcare cuts, slashed services, and tax hikes.
STOPS SACRAMENTO POLITICIANS FROM OVERSPENDING-Proposition 2 does not give Sacramento any new money to spend. On the contrary, it doubles the state’s reserve requirement and forces more savings-rather than new spending-when tax revenues spike.
PROTECTS SCHOOLS, PUBLIC SAFETY, AND HEALTHCARE-When the economy slows, Proposition 2 helps protect funding for schools, hospitals, health clinics, and public safety instead of placing them first in line for cuts. The theoretical “rebate” opponents refer to relies on a 50-year-old accounting gimmick that rewards spending instead of saving. Proposition 2 closes that loophole and mandates a real 20% Rainy Day Fund.
Don’t be fooled by those who call themselves “watchdogs.” California’s official nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office has recommended that the state expand the Rainy Day Fund to prevent boom-and-bust budget cycles. That’s why Proposition 2 is backed by the California Professional Firefighters, small business advocates, health clinics, hospitals, and education leaders-people who understand what happens when reserves run dry.
VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 2- www.YesonProp2.com
Dr. Linda Darling-Hammond , President
California State Board of Education
Carmela Coyle , CEO
California Hospital Association
Francisco J. Silva , CEO
California Primary Care Association

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Proposition 2: Rainy Day Fund
Proposition 2: Rainy Day Fund
Proposition 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment
Additional Titles
Budget Stabilization Account Cap Increase and Gann Limit Changes Amendment
Rainy day Fund
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
Summary
Proposition 2 was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email) The amendment was introduced on June 25, 2026 and it passed the state Assembly by a vote of 59-8, with 12 not voting. It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codesTOCSelected.xhtml?tocCode=CONS&tocTitle=+California+Constitution+-+CONS) by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies. Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
It would also expand the types of state debt that can be repaid with General Fund money set aside each year and require the extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of the current date of 2030). In addition, Prop. 2 would change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending cap, or “Gann Limit (https://www.cde.ca.gov/fg/ac/gl/),” making it easier to save more money when revenues are strong. The Legislature placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot through Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20).
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 2 would allow California to build a larger financial cushion by raising the maximum size of the state’s rainy day fund. It would also direct a greater share of unusually strong revenues into savings during high-revenue years. Having more money set aside could give the state greater flexibility during economic downturns or other periods when tax collections fall short of expectations.
Proposition 2 would extend requirements for additional state debt payments through 2040. As a result, California could pay down more of its outstanding debts and long-term financial obligations than it otherwise would under current rules.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s rainy day fund rules to allow larger reserves, increase deposits when revenues are strong, extend required debt payments through 2040, and change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending limit. It would also allow the governor’s May budget revision to serve as a declaration of a budget emergency when certain conditions are met.
NO: A “no” vote opposes these changes and would keep the current rules for the state’s rainy day fund, extra debt payments, spending limit, and declarations of budget emergencies.

Proposition 2 : Larger state rainy day fund
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 2 would change the State Constitution so the state keeps saving in its main rainy day fund until the fund equals 20% of General Fund taxes, up from 10% today, and saves more in years when revenue from investment gains is very high. It would also extend required extra debt payments from 2030 to 2040 and stop counting rainy day fund deposits toward the state spending limit until the money is taken out.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 2 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/).

Money raised For: $383,715.57 from July 1 to Nov. 1, 2026, by one committee controlled by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel. Against: no committee
Outside spending Against: $40,500 by Reform California (shared with other props). For: about $70,000, mostly shared with other props
Latest public poll PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 61% yes, 38% no (likely voters)
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are from state campaign filings in the Secretary of State's Cal-Access database.

What does a yes vote on Proposition 2 mean?
Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
What does a no vote on Proposition 2 mean?
Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
What would Proposition 2 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says state budget reserves would be higher, which would make it somewhat easier to balance the budget when revenue falls. The state might also make more debt payments than it would otherwise. The analysis gives no dollar figure.
What it means for the City of LA
Proposition 2 changes only state accounts. It does not change the City of Los Angeles's own reserve rules or spending limit, and the Legislative Analyst does not estimate any local effect. Its effect on the City would come through the state budget, which pays for programs the City relies on, such as state homelessness grants. A larger state reserve is meant to make state cuts less likely in a downturn, but the measure does not guarantee any program's funding.
The details
Official title Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Legislative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the Legislature (ACA 20, Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026)
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. Under the State Constitution (Article XVIII, Section 4), an amendment takes effect if "approved by a majority of votes cast thereon."
The question on your ballot
Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal Impact: State budget reserves would be higher. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel Opponents: None submitted
This is not the Proposition 2 on the November 5, 2024 ballot, the bond for public school and college facilities, which passed with 58.7% of the vote (Secretary of State, November 2024 Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-general/sov/59-state-ballot-measures.pdf)).
What would change
Today If Proposition 2 passes
Rainy day fund cap Deposits stop once the fund reaches 10% of General Fund taxes; money that would have gone in must go to infrastructure (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)) Deposits continue until the fund reaches 20% (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm))
Yearly set-aside 1.5% of General Fund tax revenue, half to the rainy day fund and half to debt payments, plus extra when capital gains revenue tops 8% of General Fund taxes (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)) The 1.5% stays. Capital gains revenue between 8% and 10% of General Fund taxes still counts as extra; above 10%, 1.5 times the amount counts (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/); text, Sec. 20 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1))
Extra debt payments Required through 2030, and only for state pension and retiree health debts (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)) Required through 2040. Can also go to money owed to schools and community colleges, loans from other state funds, and federal unemployment insurance loans (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm))
State spending limit (Gann limit) Money put into the rainy day fund counts toward the limit when deposited (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)) Starting in 2027-28, deposits do not count; withdrawals count when taken out. The same applies to the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, up to 10% of General Fund taxes a year (text, Sec. 20(i)-(j) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Declaring a budget emergency The Governor must issue a proclamation before deposits can be cut or money withdrawn (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)) The Governor’s May budget revision counts as the proclamation if it proposes cutting deposits or withdrawing money and emergency conditions exist (text, Sec. 22(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
School funding guarantee (Prop. 98) Unchanged Unchanged. The text says nothing in it “is intended to change the calculation or funding of the minimum guarantee” (text, First (b)(8) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1))
What stays the same: the state can still cut deposits or withdraw money in a budget emergency, with the same definition of emergency. No more than half the fund can be withdrawn in the first year of an emergency. Required debt payments still cannot be suspended (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
No direct change for the City. Proposition 2 amends only Sections 20 and 22 of Article XVI of the State Constitution, which govern state reserves (ACA 20 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)). The Legislative Analyst’s analysis covers only the state budget (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)).
The City’s own reserves follow City policy. The City’s Reserve Fund must equal 5% of General Fund revenue, and the City’s goal is 10% across its Reserve Fund, Budget Stabilization Fund and unappropriated balance (City 2026-27 Proposed Budget, General Fund Reserves Policy (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf#page=24)). Proposition 2 does not change these.
Indirect effect through the state budget. The City budgets state money for some programs, such as the state’s Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention (HHAP) grants (City 2026-27 Proposed Budget (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf)). The Analyst says higher reserves “would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)). The measure does not set aside money for any local program. The Budget Center says money set aside in boom years would not be available then for needs such as “support for local governments to address homelessness” (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)).
The Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce is one of the signers of the argument in favor (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/arguments-rebuttals.htm)). We found no City Council position on Proposition 2 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
ACA 20 needed a two-thirds vote of each house (ACA 20 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)). It was filed with the Secretary of State without a Governor’s signature (ACA 20 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)).
June 22, 2026: ACA 20 was introduced. Its lead authors are Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Valencia and Senators Hurtado and John Laird. The Assembly voted 51-16 to suspend two of its rules the same day (ACA 20 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20); ACA 20 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)).
June 25, 2026: The Assembly tabled amendments offered by Assemblymember David Tangipa, 55-18, then adopted ACA 20, 59-8. The Senate withdrew it from committee and adopted it the same day, 29-2. It was filed as Resolution Chapter 130 (ACA 20 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20); ACA 20 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)). The Assembly no votes were DeMaio, Dixon, Ellis, Hadwick, Macedo, Patterson, Sanchez and Tangipa. The Senate no votes were Choi and Grove (ACA 20 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)).
The Governor’s office listed the amendment as part of the 2026-27 budget agreement announced June 26 (Governor’s office (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/06/26/finalbudget/)). The Assembly Budget Committee’s floor report says the rainy day fund changes were “completed in conjunction with legislative approval of ACA 20” (Assembly floor report, p. 6 (https://abgt.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-06/floor-report-of-the-2026-27-budget-june-27-2026_5.pdf#page=6)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. The State Constitution says a proposed amendment “shall be submitted to the electors and, if approved by a majority of votes cast thereon, takes effect” (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).
Related past measures.
Proposition 58 (2004) created the rainy day fund, the Budget Stabilization Account (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)).
Proposition 2 (November 2014) set the current deposit, debt payment and 10% cap rules (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)). It passed with 69.1% statewide and 69.8% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2014 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2014-general/pdf/88-ballot-measures.pdf)).
Proposition 4 (1979) created the state spending limit, known as the Gann limit (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument in favor, signed by Darrell Roberts of California Professional Firefighters, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel and Maria S. Salinas of the Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
The state budget swung “from a $100 billion surplus to a $50 billion deficit in just a few years.”
It doubles the reserve requirement “so California has a real cushion.”
It makes the state bank more of a revenue spike “instead of committing it to new ongoing spending.”
The Legislative Analyst “has recommended that the state should be saving significantly more than current rules require.”
Their rebuttal, signed by Linda Darling-Hammond of the State Board of Education, Carmela Coyle of the California Hospital Association and Francisco J. Silva of the California Primary Care Association, calls the taxpayer rebate “a 50-year-old accounting gimmick that rewards spending instead of saving” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by Assemblymember David Tangipa, Sen. Steven Choi and Carl DeMaio of Reform California (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
It lets politicians “gut the voter-imposed spending limit” and creates a “SLUSH FUND.”
It “cancels your tax rebate,” which the Constitution requires when revenue exceeds the spending limit.
The state budget “has grown by 76% since 2018.”
“Within 24 hours” of putting it on the ballot, the same politicians “voted to suspend more than $5 billion in required deposits.”
Outside the guide.
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association recommends a no vote. Its guide says the measure’s reserve changes make sense “from the perspective of addressing revenue volatility” but calls it “little more than a Band-Aid on a severed limb” because it does not undo earlier changes to the Gann limit (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)).
Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón said the budget deal addresses “our short and long-term financial future by building up our rainy day fund” (Governor’s office (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/06/26/finalbudget/)).

California’s ‘orphaned’ ballot measures
By WILL MCCARTHY (https://www.politico.com/staff/will-mccarthy), JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white) and NICOLE NORMAN (https://www.politico.com/staff/nicole-norman)
10/05/2026 03:09 PM EDT
State Sen. Josh Newman talks during a Senate session in Sacramento, California, on June 11, 2018. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
LEFT BEHIND: Over the last two and a half years, California lawmakers spent countless hours drafting, debating and voting on a group of government reform ballot measures to put before voters. The same energy has not been put toward campaigns to pass them.
Proposition 5, which would change how successors are chosen in recalls, was set for the ballot way back in August 2024. Proposition 4, which would allow for the public financing of campaigns, landed in October 2025. Proposition 2, which would double the amount the state can deposit into its reserves, was rushed to the November ballot earlier this spring.
All aim to reform a somewhat wonky aspect of how government operates, and none of them are easily explainable to voters in a single sentence. And yet each of them have a limited, or non-existent public presence and campaign.
“You get these orphaned initiatives,” said Thad Kousser , a professor of political science at the University of San Diego. “So voters are left with very few bits of information on what’s going to be the most crowded ballot in a decade.”
The recall measure’s travails underscore how quickly a political window can close. In the aftermath of the failed attempt to recall Gov. Gavin Newsom , triumphant Democrats said they were determined to change a system that would allow a challenger — like MAGA tribune Larry Elder (https://www.politico.com/news/2021/08/17/ca-recall-election-larry-elder-505735) — to become governor with fewer votes than the number cast against a recall. Secretary of State Shirley Weber vowed action (https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/09/15/california-elections-chief-wants-recall-overhaul-possibly-as-soon-as-2022-1391082), and election committees revved up (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2021/09/16/with-newsom-secure-democrats-look-to-restrain-recall-494353).
But the momentum soon ebbed. Policymakers couldn’t agree on the changes. Polls showed voters were tepid on changing a process that many see as an important check on elected officials. By the time former State Sen. Josh Newman finally got his measure through, the Newsom recall — and the sense of urgency it engendered — were distant memories.
A spokesperson for the Prop 5 campaign did not reply to requests for comment, although Newman said in a recent interview that he was “not optimistic” about the recall reform measure’s chances.
Historically, the vast majority of measures placed on the ballot by the legislature have won — a full 69% between 1910 and 2025. In the past, that outcome has been largely a function of how many votes it takes for lawmakers to put measures before voters, a two-thirds majority of both houses traditionally meaning that the issue was highly popular.
But polling for the three government reform measures is scattershot. A September Public Policy Institute of California poll had Prop 4 and Prop 5 with only 42% and 35% support, respectively, while Prop 2 had the support of 60% of voters (a later Berkeley IGS poll put Prop 4’s support at 35% for, 35% against, and 30% undecided).
Prop 5 does not appear to have any financial backing or a campaign committee organized to pass the measure. The committee for Prop 4 has a single, $235,000 contribution from Movement Voter PAC, a progressive organizing group. Prop 2’s committee received a $150,000 contribution from Google last week.
Assemblymember Alex Lee , one of the coauthors of the legislation that placed Prop 4 on the ballot, said the measure was in a “good place” and that undecided voters are “ready to be persuaded.” The Prop 4 campaign has begun holding public events and is planning a bus tour at some point this fall.
“I knew the other marquee efforts would absorb the media attention,” Lee said. “Really it’s just about the voter education campaign.”
Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel , author of Prop 2, said you likely won’t see large ad spends or public appearances to drum up support for expanding the state’s budget reserves. Given the solid polling and what he called the “common sense wisdom” of the measure, he’s confident in its passage.
Meant to shield the state’s budget from the volatility of the stock market, the measure has the support of a wide range of groups, from the California Chamber of Commerce to SEIU. Even so, Gabriel said he expected a “lean campaign” that will “rely a lot on member-to-member communication.”
Each of the government reform measures share at least one key advantage: None face organized opposition.
“Its not like we have to raise X millions of dollars,” Lee said.
Welcome to Ballot Measure Weekly , a special Monday edition of Playbook PM focused on California’s lively realm of ballot measure campaigns. Questions? Concerns? Tips? Drop ballot measures reporter Will McCarthy a line at [email protected] (https://www.politico.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#65120806060417110d1c25150a090c110c060a4b060a08) .
TOP OF THE TICKET
A highly subjective ranking of the ballot measures — past and future, certain and possible — getting our attention this week.
1. Prop 37: The campaign for a measure to provide loans to help middle-income families purchase homes contributed $300,000 to the California Democratic Party last week, apparently viewing the measure in good financial standing.
2. Prop 38: The No on Prop 38 campaign is operating with a single six-figure check as it tries to run a campaign against billionaire Gary Michelson ’s immunology bond ballot measure. The $3,000 contribution comes from Robert Kaplan , the director of research at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center. Michelson has contributed over $10 million to the initiative, which has come under criticism in recent weeks (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).
3. Prop 45: A group of Republican county organizations came out against Prop 45 last week, even as the Yes campaign faced scrutiny for donations (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317427465.html) to Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio ’s Reform California organization (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730). The Yes campaign, meanwhile, released a report (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/) showing what it says would be the “significant economic benefits” of Prop 45, including adding 20,000 homes a year.
4. Fund scientific research (2028): Newsom climbed the Golden Gate Bridge (https://x.com/CAgovernor/status/2105470383281598682) with State Sen. Scott Wiener and a camera crew to sign a $7.5 billion research bond that aims to combat federal funding cuts. The measure will be on the ballot in 2028. “I’m proud to sign a bond to invest in the future of the state of California,” Newsom said in a video from the bridge.
5. Prop 40: Heavily outspent and facing enormous establishment resistance, the wealth tax campaign is hoping America’s most prominent progressive can carry it to victory. Sen. Bernie Sanders is rallying for Prop 40 in Los Angeles today after swinging through San Francisco on Saturday, where he described the campaign as a Democrat-defining battle over “the most important ballot initiative in the country.” (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/03/bernie-sanders-billionaire-tax-san-francisco-rally-01105995)
6. Prop 39: DeMaio is continuing on his “Barbecue, Beer, & Ballots” tour through California, attending his tenth barbecue of the last week in Ramona (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/events/barbeque-beer-ballots-ramona-10-05-2026) today as the campaign looks to help pass Prop 39. As Will wrote for POLITICO Magazine last week (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730?utm_source=firefox-newtab-en-us), DeMaio’s grassroots army has become a major factor in his rise in state politics.
7. Measure ER (Los Angeles County): A one-half cent sales tax narrowly approved by Los Angeles County voters in June took effect on Oct. 1. But it could be a while before the $1 billion it is expected to generate each year for health care can actually be spent. A lawsuit, brought by the Libertarian Party of LA County, will have to play out in LA County Superior Court before the proceeds can be used.
FIRST IN PLAYBOOK — Californians for Voting Rights, one of the committees organized to defeat Prop 39, is launching a pair of advertisements in the Bay Area hammering on the “consequences voters will face” should the measure pass. In the first spot, the No campaign characterizes Prop 39 as a “MAGA power grab” led by President Donald Trump (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cjk5YyP7FYM). The second warns people (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EbT1lgt8ic4) of longer lines in order to vote. The seven-figure buy is the committee’s first time on air.
IN OTHER NEWS
HE’S BACK: Former Gov. Jerry Brown will tonight join journalist Miriam Pawel , the author of nonfiction works about the Brown family (https://miriampawel.com/the-browns-of-california/) and Cesar Chavez (https://www.nytimes.com/2014/04/27/books/review/the-crusades-of-cesar-chavez-by-miriam-pawel.html), for a conversation launching her latest book: “California Dreams: The Making and Remaking of the University of California.” The discussion will “explore the history of the University of California, its relationship with California’s political and social life, and the continuing importance of public higher education,” and the event will run from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. at the California State Library. The retired Brown’s appearance is his latest since he visited the state Capitol during end-of-session proceedings and penned a call for global nuclear (https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2026/10/08/i-taste-ashes-in-the-wind-nuclear-weapons-jerry-brown/) disarmament. Register here (https://libraryca.libcal.com/event/17654368) .
THE BOOGEYMAN: Democrats’ top Senate super PAC is flooding the airwaves with ads hitting Republicans on Jeffrey Epstein, the late financier and convicted sex offender. They have data to back it up, POLITICO’s Andrew Howard reports (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/05/democrats-smp-attack-ads-epstein-01106408).
Internal polling of over 4,500 voters from Senate Majority PAC, conducted by the Democratic firm Blue Rose Research late last week and shared with POLITICO, found that a 44% plurality of voters — including the same percentage of swing voters — think the Epstein issue is “serious” and that Republicans should be held responsible.
And while nothing trumps affordability as the issue du jour on the campaign trail this fall, state-level research from SMP found that the Epstein ads can shift races three to six points in Democrats’ direction.

What your vote means
Yes
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.

Arguments
Pro
Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
Con
Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.

Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund.
Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
#### Reserves
***State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.”*** The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state’s main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year.
Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program.
In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal.
During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
***Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level.*** Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits.
The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).
...
